queries.hook: The wish to understand what these texts teach, and to find in them something steady to lean on.
queries.diagnose: When life is lived only for what passes, the heart feels empty; meaning is missing when we forget what does not pass.
queries.steady: What passes cannot fill the heart; turning toward what lasts gives each day a quiet purpose.
queries.act: Turn toward what lasts: serve, study, reflect daily, and offer your work to something beyond yourself.
queries.story: A story of a student who came to a teacher with questions and was led, step by step, toward the truth.

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on simple, wholehearted devotion.
verse.sanskrit: पत्रं पुष्पं फलं तोयं यो मे भक्त्या प्रयच्छति । तदहं भक्त्युपहृतमश्नामि प्रयतात्मनः ॥

verse.translation: Whoever offers me with devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit or water, that offering of love from the pure-hearted I accept.
verse.why: Small offerings given with love matter; no one is beyond turning around.

prasang.title: The glory of selfless devotion
prasang.summary: A leaf, flower, fruit or water offered with love is accepted. Offer everything you do; the divine hates no one, and even a wrongdoer who turns wholeheartedly is counted good.
prasang.lesson: Small offerings given with love matter; no one is beyond turning around.

verse.meaning: Krishna is speaking to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna has asked what kind of people worship the divine and how. Krishna answers that the divine does not need grand rituals or expensive gifts. A simple leaf, a flower, a fruit, or even a little water, given with love and devotion, is fully accepted. This means that no one is too small or too flawed to offer something real. The act of giving, not the value of the gift, is what matters.
verse.for_you: The map you used to follow has run out, and now you are standing in a quiet room with no instructions. You do not need to build a new temple to find meaning.
verse.scene_line: You are standing in your quiet house, offering the morning light and a cup of tea to the silence, and that is a full prayer.
asks: How do I offer my days when they feel so empty?
What does it mean to give with love when I feel nothing?

verse.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse.setting: From the section on wealth: how need changes what we value.
verse.sanskrit: परिक्षीणः कश्चित्स्पृहयति यवानां प्रसृतये स पश्चात् सम्पूर्णः कलयति धरित्रीं तृणसमाम् । अतश्चानैकान्त्याद्गुरुलघुतयाऽर्थेषु धनिना- मवस्था वस्तूनि प्रथयति च सङ्कोचयति च ॥
verse.line: Starving, a handful of grain is everything. Full, the whole earth looks like straw.
verse.translation: A man who has lost everything longs for a handful of barley; later, when full, he counts the whole earth as straw. Because nothing is fixed, a person's condition makes things look great or small.
verse.why: Money changes how others see you, not who you are. Give it, enjoy it, or lose it.

prasang.title: Nitishatakam: On wealth
prasang.summary: A wry look at money: how the world flatters the rich and forgets the broke, wealth's three destinies, and how distance and neglect ruin what we value. It closes with advice to the chataka bird not to plead before every cloud.
prasang.lesson: Money changes how others see you, not who you are. Give it, enjoy it, or lose it.

verse.meaning: Bhartrihari speaks to the reader from the section on wealth, looking at how need changes what we value. He says that a man who has lost everything longs for a handful of barley. Later, when full, he counts the whole earth as straw. Because nothing is fixed, a person's condition makes things look great or small.
verse.for_you: Your days now hold more than enough, yet the old habit of needing a grand purpose still makes the room feel hollow. The value you once gave to a title or a project has shifted. What looks like straw to you now is the quiet ground beneath your feet.
verse.try_today: Notice one small thing you do not need to earn or prove.
verse.scene_line: You sit in a full room and count the whole earth as straw.
asks: How do I see value in a life that no longer needs a title?
What if the straw I see is actually the ground I stand on?
How do I stop needing the whole earth to feel full?

verse.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse.setting: From 'The Mockery of Giving Up Pleasures'.
verse.sanskrit: अवश्यं यातारश्चिरतरमुषित्वापि विषया वियोगे को भेदस्त्यजति न जनो यत्स्वयममून् । व्रजन्तः स्वातन्त्र्यादतुलपरितापाय मनसः स्वयं त्यक्ता ह्येते शमसुखमनन्तं विदधति ॥
verse.line: Every pleasure leaves someday. Released freely, it brings peace; torn away, it brings torment.
verse.translation: Pleasures will certainly leave, however long they stay with us. Then what difference is there in parting? Only that people do not let them go themselves. Leaving of their own accord, they bring the mind unequalled torment; given up by oneself, they bring endless peace.
verse.why: Let go before you are forced to, and stop calling relief happiness.
verse.misuse: About things and pleasures; not advice to leave people before they leave you.

prasang.title: Vairagyashatakam: The mockery of giving up pleasures
prasang.summary: Pleasures will leave us anyway; letting them go freely brings peace, being dragged from them brings torment. We are worse than the moth, because we know the flame burns.
prasang.lesson: Let go before you are forced to, and stop calling relief happiness.

verse.meaning: Bhartrihari speaks to the reader from his text on the mockery of giving up pleasures. He says that all pleasures will leave us eventually, no matter how long they stay. The only difference is how we let them go. If we force them away, we suffer. If we release them freely, we find endless peace.
verse.for_you: Turn inward, come to know the self, and let your work become service and offering; a life lived from there is full.
verse.try_today: Notice one small thing you are holding onto and let it go.
verse.scene_line: You are at the edge of a room with the door already open.
asks: How do I release what I have built?
Can I let go of my own accord?

verse.speaker: Prajapati's teaching (narrator)
verse.setting: On the self in the heart that we visit nightly in deep sleep without knowing it.
verse.sanskrit: अनृतापिधानास्तद्यथापि हिरण्यनिधिं निहितमक्षेत्रज्ञा उपर्युपरि सञ्चरन्तो न विन्देयुरेवमेवेमाः सर्वाः प्रजा अहरहर्गच्छन्त्य एतं ब्रह्मलोकं न विन्दन्त्यनृतेन हि प्रत्यूढाः ॥
verse.line: Like people walking daily over buried gold, we pass our own treasure every day and never find it.
verse.translation: As people who do not know the spot walk again and again over a hidden treasure of gold buried in the ground and do not find it, so all these creatures go day after day into that world of Brahman and do not find it, for they are carried away by untruth.

matched.label: Nothing is wrong but nothing feels meaningful

verse.meaning: The narrator is describing the self that lives in the heart and is visited every night in deep sleep. People walk over buried gold every day and do not see it. In the same way, all living beings go into that world of Brahman and pass it by, carried away by untruth.
verse.for_you: You have spent a lifetime building a life that is now complete. You are walking over the one thing you were looking for without knowing it. The treasure is not a new project or a new role. It is the self that has always been here.
verse.try_today: Sit still for a moment and feel what is already inside you.
verse.scene_line: You walk over your own treasure every day and never find it.
asks: How do I know the treasure is inside me?
How do I stop walking over what I have?

verse.speaker: Vasishtha
verse.setting: Vasishtha, after Janaka's story, praises clear understanding (prajna).
verse.sanskrit: य एव यत्नः क्रियते बाह्यार्थोपार्जने जनैः । स एव यत्नः कर्तव्यः पूर्वं प्रज्ञाविवर्धने ॥
verse.line: Put the effort you spend earning money into growing wiser first.
verse.translation: The very effort people put into earning outer wealth should first be put into growing wisdom.
verse.why: You don't have to leave your life to change it. Do the day's work with a mind that doesn't clutch.

prasang.title: King Janaka overhears the sages and keeps ruling, with a free mind
prasang.summary: Walking in his spring garden, King Janaka overhears hidden sages singing about the self. Shaken, he climbs to his palace roof and questions everything he has lived for. When his doorkeeper calls him to the day's work, he decides not to run away: he gets up and does his duties, but with a mind that no longer clutches.
prasang.story_hook: One spring morning, a king out for a walk overheard a song that he could not stop thinking about.
prasang.lesson: You don't have to leave your life to change it. Do the day's work with a mind that doesn't clutch.

verse.meaning: Vasishtha speaks to Rama after a long talk about King Janaka. Janaka had been ruling his kingdom, but he heard hidden sages singing about the self. He climbed to his palace roof and questioned everything he had lived for. Then his doorkeeper called him to the day's work. He decided not to run away. He got up and did his duties, but with a mind that no longer clutches.
verse.for_you: You have spent a lifetime earning what the world calls success. Now the gold is here and the search is over. You can still tend to your days, but let the old clutch go. Let the morning paper or the evening walk be enough without proving anything.
verse.try_today: Do one small task today with a mind that does not clutch.
verse.scene_line: You are walking in your own spring garden and hearing the hidden song of what remains.
asks: How do I let go of the need to prove anything now?
What does it mean to do my duties with a free mind?
How do I know when I am clutching and when I am simply living?

verse.speaker: Seer
verse.setting: Follows the call to enjoy by letting go: how to live and work.
verse.sanskrit: कुर्वन्नेवेह कर्माणि जिजीविषेच्छतꣳ समाः । एवं त्वयि नान्यथेतोऽस्ति न कर्म लिप्यते नरे ॥
verse.line: Do your work and wish to live a full hundred years. Done in this spirit, action does not cling.
verse.translation: Doing your work here, you may wish to live a hundred years. For you there is no other way than this: done in this spirit, action does not cling to a person.
verse.why: Hold what you have lightly, keep working, and see yourself in everyone.

prasang.title: The Isha: enjoy by letting go
prasang.summary: Eighteen verses that open by saying everything belongs to the divine, so we should enjoy it without grasping. They go on to say we should work a full life without being bound, and see ourselves in all beings.
prasang.lesson: Hold what you have lightly, keep working, and see yourself in everyone.

verse.meaning: A seer speaks to a reader who is trying to live well in the world. They say, do your work, and wish to live a full hundred years. For you there is no other way. Done in this spirit, action does not cling. The verse tells you to hold what you have lightly, keep working, and see yourself in everyone. It is a call to work with a full heart but without the weight of grasping, so that your life remains open and unburdened.
verse.for_you: You are in a time when the old reasons for working have faded, yet the days still ask for your attention. This verse does not ask you to do more, but to do what remains with a lighter hand.
verse.try_today: Notice one small task and do it with your full attention.
verse.scene_line: You are at the start of a long morning, and the work before you is yours to do.
asks: How do I do my work without it clinging to me?
What does it mean to see myself in everyone today?
Is there a small task I can do with a lighter hand?

story.title: Satyakama Jabala, the honest boy
story.story_hook: Satyakama wanted to study, but first he had to ask his mother a question she could not answer.
story.summary: A boy who wants to study asks his mother about his father's lineage. She tells him frankly she does not know, and he repeats this word for word to the teacher. The teacher accepts him for his honesty, sends him off with 400 weak cows, and the boy returns years later with a thousand, having learned from nature along the way, yet still asks his teacher to teach him.
story.lesson: Honesty about who you are is the best credential you can bring.

anchor.speaker: Jabala
anchor.setting: A boy asks his mother his lineage before seeking a teacher.
anchor.sanskrit: सा हैनमुवाच नाहमेतद्वेद तात यद्गोत्रस्त्वमसि बह्वहं चरन्ती परिचारिणी यौवने त्वामलभे साहमेतन्न वेद यद्गोत्रस्त्वमसि जबाला तु नामाहमस्मि सत्यकामो नाम त्वमसि स सत्यकाम एव जाबालो ब्रवीथा इति ॥
anchor.line: His mother said, 'I don't know your father's line. I am Jabala, you are Satyakama. Say exactly that.'
anchor.translation: She said to him: 'I do not know your lineage, my child. In my youth I moved about a great deal as a serving woman, and then I had you. So I do not know your lineage. My name is Jabala and your name is Satyakama. Just say you are Satyakama Jabala.'
anchor.why: Honesty about who you are is the best credential you can bring.

story.hook_title: A boy didn't know who his father was, and told his teacher the truth anyway
story.teaser: A boy didn't know who his father was, and told his teacher the truth anyway
story.for_you: You stand at the edge of a new chapter, not because a door closed, but because the map you carried no longer points to a destination. The search for what it is all for is not a failure of the last forty years.
asks: What do I know for certain about who I am?
How does naming my truth change what I do next?
What is the first step on the path I can name?
